en: One term you'll frequently encounter when
working with large language models,
especially when working with AI agents, is
the term context window.
And a model's context window is simply the
maximum amount of
tokens
it can hold and it can send as input to the
model to produce new output. So for example,
if you're asking a model to summarize a long
PDF document with lots of text in there,
all that text has to be split up into tokens
and has to be sent to the model.
And then you get back a response. You may
send a follow-up question. And for the next
term where the model should answer the
follow-up question, it needs the full
context, which means the original text you
sent in your first message,
then also its response so that it knows what
it already told you, and then your follow-up
question.
And that altogether makes up the so-called
context window. All of that is the so-called
context you're sending to the model. Which
it gets to produce its next answer. Now,
those models, those large language models,
have limited context windows because they
are not able to
process endless amounts of text. And indeed,
they tend to produce worse results if you
send
lots and lots of text to them, which is
another reason for why we have these context
windows, because the model providers
realized that from a certain point on, you
would not be getting back good results. And
therefore they rather restrict you and don't
allow you to send endless amounts of text
instead of you getting back bad results. So
whenever you hear the term context window,
we're simply talking about the information,
the tokens you're sending to a model in the
end, and the potential limit for that
context window that may be enforced by the
model or by the provider of that model.
It's also worth noting that in that context
window, you don't just have the text you may
be seeing in your AI agent or in ChatGPT or
whatever you're using, but there also is
some invisible stuff in there, potentially.
Things like a so-called system instruction
where, for example, if you're using ChatGPT,
OpenAI, the provider of ChatGPT, may have
some invisible instructions in there to, for
example, always answer in a friendly way or
things like
So these are instructions you don't see,
which are sent to the model nonetheless.
So your context window typically won't be
empty, even if you have not sent a single
word to the model yet.
